words: push; pull; strong; gentle; direction; move; stop; roll
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare which push made the ball go farther)
notes: The first investigation of the year, so it also teaches the K-2 observing practice every later row uses: notice with the senses and a hand lens, say what you notice and wonder, record with a labelled drawing, a tally or a dot on a class chart. Then plan and carry out, with the class, a test of what a bigger or smaller push or pull does to how an object moves, and what pushing from a different direction does: a ball rolled with a gentle and a strong push, a box pulled by a string, a rolling ball stopped by a hand, two balls bumping. Students compare which went farther or faster in relative words. The reasoning that grows: a push or pull causes a change in motion, and a bigger push causes a bigger change (introduces cause-effect). Boundary: only strength or direction is varied in one test, never both at once; only contact pushes and pulls, no magnets. Teacher note: rolling and pulling stays on the floor in a cleared space; no throwing; no tasting or sniffing unknown things during observation.

words: ramp; speed; faster; slower; turn; path; works; test
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare distances and speeds directly)
notes: A design problem: make a ball or marble roll a set distance, follow a path, turn a corner or knock down a target, using ramps, blocks, books and card walls. Students try a solution, watch whether it does what was wanted and use simple results (did it reach the line, yes or no; which ramp sent it farther) to decide whether the design works as intended. The reasoning that grows: a designed object changes speed or direction by pushing on the ball, and a test tells whether it works. Boundary: friction is not taught as the reason a ball slows. Uses the design steps from sk-define-problem. Teacher note: marbles are a choking hazard for some kindergarten children; use larger balls or close supervision.

words: sunlight; shade; warm; warmer; cool; cooler; surface
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare two surfaces: warmer or cooler)
notes: Observe that sunlight warms the Earth's surface: touch sand, soil, rocks and a pan of water in the sun and in the shade, morning and afternoon, and record which is warmer. The reasoning that grows: sunlight causes the warming, so the same thing in shade is cooler. Boundary: temperature only in relative words (warmer, cooler); no thermometer readings are required. Teacher note: dark surfaces such as pavement or metal can be hot enough to hurt; the teacher checks first and students touch with the back of a hand briefly; never look at the sun.

words: problem; solve; design; build; idea; tool
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.3 (ask questions to get information about the problem)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-1, done in full here: before building, students ask questions, observe and gather information about a situation people want to change, and say the problem in one sentence ("The slide is too hot to use after lunch"; "The ball will not reach the bin"). Introduces the design-cycle as three steps a kindergartner can say: what is the problem, try an idea, test it. Practised through the kindergarten design problems (sk-ramp-design, sk-shade-design, sk-reduce-impact) rather than as a separate unit. Grade 1 adds a sketch of how shape helps function (s1-sketch-shape); grade 2 adds comparing two designs by test data (s2-compare-designs). Later grades redefine the problem with criteria and constraints (grades 3 to 5).

words: shade; structure; block; cover; umbrella; tent
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare the spot under the shade with a spot in the sun)
notes: Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a small area (a shade for a toy animal, a sandbox corner or an ice cube), then test it by comparing the shaded spot with one in the sun. The reasoning that grows: blocking sunlight causes less warming, so the material and shape of the cover matter. Uses sk-sun-warms and the design steps of sk-define-problem. Boundary: relative warmer or cooler only. Teacher note: scissors are child-safe; check surfaces before touching as in sk-sun-warms.

words: living; need; food; water; air; light; plant; animal; survive
cross_subject: math:K.MD.B.3 (sort living things into groups and count each group)
notes: Use observations of class plants, a class animal or schoolyard life, pictures and video to describe patterns in what plants and animals, people included, need to survive: all need water; animals take in food and plants do not; different animals eat different foods (some eat plants, some eat other animals); plants need light. Introduces the patterns model: the same thing seen again and again across many living things. Boundary: no photosynthesis, no food chains; plants making their own food is grade 5. Handoff to s2-plant-needs-test skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no plant-needs expectation; grade 2 tests the need for light and water by experiment. Teacher note: class animals are cared for humanely and handled only with an adult; check food and pet allergies before any animal or animal food comes into the room.

words: weather; sunny; cloudy; rainy; windy; warm; cool; chart; pattern
cross_subject: math:K.MD.B.3 (count sunny, cloudy and rainy days and sort the counts)
notes: Observe and record local weather each day on a class chart (sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy; warmer or cooler), then share and read the chart for patterns over time: it is usually cooler in the morning than the afternoon; one month had more sunny days than another. Introduces data-graph as a class picture graph or tally chart, and patterns over time, using the observing and recording habits begun in sk-push-pull. Boundary: counts are whole numbers and temperature is relative (warmer, cooler). Keep the chart all year so grade 1 sky and daylight work can lean on the habit.

words: forecast; storm; severe; warning; prepare; safe
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.3 (ask and answer questions to get information)
notes: Ask questions to find out why people forecast the weather: a forecast tells us severe weather may be coming so we can get ready and stay safe. Students ask a visiting adult, watch a short forecast and look at a picture book to answer their own questions, then name what the school and families do for the local kinds of severe weather (storm, blizzard, heat, flood, tornado or hurricane as fits the region). The reasoning: knowing what is coming causes people to prepare. The obtaining-information practice passes to grade 1 (reading texts and media, s1-parent-offspring); the Earth-events thread passes to grade 2 (s2-fast-slow-events), skipping grade 1 because grade 1 has no Earth-events expectation. Teacher note: severe weather can frighten young children and some have lived through a disaster; keep the focus on safety plans and helpers, and do not ask children to retell frightening events.

words: change; environment; dig; build; claim; evidence; because
cross_subject: ela:W.K.1 (draw and tell an opinion with a reason)
notes: Make a claim and back it with evidence: plants and animals, people included, change their surroundings to get what they need. Evidence from photographs, video and the schoolyard: a squirrel digs to hide food, tree roots crack a sidewalk, beavers build a dam, birds build nests, people clear land for houses. Introduces claim-evidence-reasoning at its simplest: I think ..., because I saw ... Students draw and tell, with the teacher writing. Builds on the needs patterns of sk-living-needs.

words: live; home; place; meadow; forest; pond; together; system
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.5 (add drawings to a description)
notes: Use a model (a drawing, a class diorama or a picture map) to show how what a plant or animal needs connects to where it lives: deer eat buds and leaves so they live near forests; grass needs sunlight so it grows in open meadows; fish need water so they live in ponds. Plants, animals and their surroundings together are a system (introduces system-model as parts that need each other). Uses the needs patterns of sk-living-needs. Handoff to s2-habitat-diversity skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no habitat expectation; grade 1 carries the system-model through the parts of organisms (s1-parts-mimic).

words: reuse; recycle; reduce; waste; protect; land; water; air
cross_subject: ela:W.K.2 (draw, tell and write to inform others)
notes: Communicate solutions that lessen people's effect on the local land, water, air and living things: cutting trees to make paper, using materials to make bottles, litter in the schoolyard; solutions such as reusing paper, recycling cans and bottles, a class litter pick-up. Students choose one solution, explain in drawing and words why it helps, and share it with another class or families (a poster or short talk). Uses the design steps of sk-define-problem and the cause-effect thinking of sk-sun-warms. No in-band handoff: the thread picks up in grades 3 to 5 (human impact and solutions). Teacher note: litter pick-ups use gloves and grabbers, no glass or sharp items, adults bag the waste.

words: sound; vibrate; vibration; pluck; loud; soft; tuning fork
cross_subject: ela:W.1.8 (recall information from the investigation to answer a question)
notes: Plan and carry out, with peers and teacher guidance, investigations that give evidence that vibrating materials make sound and that sound can make materials vibrate: pluck a stretched rubber band, tap a drum with rice on top, touch a humming throat, hold paper near a speaker, a tuning fork touched to water. The reasoning that grows from kindergarten: a push or pluck (sk-push-pull) sets the material moving back and forth, and that motion causes the sound. Planning grows from the class tests of sk-push-pull: students now say what they will do and what they will watch for. Boundary: no wave model, wavelength or speed of sound; waves are grade 4. Teacher note: keep sounds at classroom level and never near ears; rubber bands are held so they cannot snap toward faces; eye protection if anything can fly.

words: light; dark; see; light source; shine; illuminate
cross_subject: ela:W.1.2 (write an explanation with facts)
notes: Make observations (a dark box with a peephole, a darkened room, a video of a cave explorer with a flashlight) to build an evidence-based account that we see objects only when light shines on them, from a light source such as the sun, a lamp or a flashlight, or when the object gives off its own light. The sun from sk-sun-warms is now named as a light source. The account uses claim-evidence-reasoning from sk-change-environment, now written with a sentence frame. Boundary: no light entering the eye or reflection model; that is grade 4. Teacher note: never look at the sun or shine a light into anyone's eyes; some children fear the dark, so let them hold the flashlight or sit by the door.

words: transparent; translucent; opaque; reflect; mirror; beam; shadow
cross_subject: math:1.MD.C.4 (sort the materials into three groups and count each)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation of what happens when objects of different materials are put in a beam of light: clear plastic lets light through (transparent), wax paper lets some through (translucent), cardboard blocks it and makes a shadow (opaque), a mirror sends it a new way (reflective). The reasoning that grows from sk-shade-design: the material, not just the shape, decides how much light gets through. Planning grows from sk-push-pull: students choose the materials and keep the flashlight in the same place. Boundary: no speed of light. Teacher note: mirrors are plastic or edge-taped; no lasers.

words: signal; message; send; receive; distance; device; code
cross_subject: math:1.MD.A.2 (measure how far the signal reached in length units)
notes: Use tools and materials to design and build a device that uses light or sound to send a message across a distance: a cup-and-string telephone, a flashlight blink code, a pattern of drum beats. Students define the problem (sk-define-problem), build, then test whether the message got through at a longer distance, as in sk-ramp-design they judge whether the design works as intended. Uses the sound and light ideas of this year. Strand engineering because the expectation is a design task. Boundary: no technical details of how phones or radios work. Teacher note: string under tension at face height is a trip and eye hazard; flashlights are never pointed at eyes.

words: root; stem; leaf; flower; fruit; shell; claw; part; job; mimic; protect
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.2 (find the main topic and key details in an informational text)
notes: Two moves in one expectation. First the core idea: plants and animals have outside parts that help them survive, grow and meet their needs (roots take in water and hold the plant, leaves face the light, a turtle's shell protects it, a hawk's eyes find food), and animals sense and respond to what is around them. Students observe real plants, pictures and video and record part and job in a two-column chart. This builds on sk-living-needs (what living things need) and sk-needs-places (the system-model): each living thing is itself made of parts that work together. Introduces structure-function: the shape of a part fits its job. Then the design that completes 1-LS1-1: use materials to solve a human problem by copying how a plant or animal uses its parts (a helmet like a turtle shell or acorn cap, a stand that will not tip like roots or a tail, a fence with spikes like thorns, an alarm that hears like big ears). Students define the human problem (sk-define-problem) and build; the planned sketch is the work of s1-sketch-shape. Teacher note: no handling of wild animals; plant parts are not tasted.

words: sketch; drawing; label; model; shape; plan
cross_subject: ela:SL.1.5 (add drawings to make an idea clear)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-2, done in full here: develop a simple sketch, labelled drawing or physical model to show how the shape of an object helps it work to solve a given problem, and use it to explain the design to others. Practised through s1-parts-mimic (shape copied from nature) and s1-signal-device (cup shape, string length). In kindergarten students built and showed (sk-ramp-design, sk-shade-design) without a planned sketch; grade 2 tests two such designs against each other with data (s2-compare-designs). The design-cycle grows a step: problem, sketch, build, test.

words: parent; offspring; young; protect; feed; signal; cry
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.1 (ask and answer questions about key details in a text)
notes: Read texts and use media (picture books, short video) to find patterns in how parents and young behave to help the young survive: the young signal (crying, cheeping, calling) and parents respond (feeding, comforting, carrying, protecting). The obtaining-information practice grows from sk-forecast-severe: now students read and compare more than one source for the same pattern. Teacher note: families differ (one parent, grandparents, foster and adoptive families); keep examples to animals and never ask a child to describe their own family.

words: alike; different; young; parent; same kind; trait
cross_subject: math:1.MD.A.1 (order leaves by length)
notes: Make observations to build an evidence-based account that young plants and animals are like, but not exactly like, their parents: leaves from one kind of plant share a shape but differ in size; puppies look like their parents but not exactly. Students line up leaves by length and compare photographs of animal families. claim-evidence-reasoning grows from sk-change-environment: the claim now rests on measured or listed differences. Boundary: no inheritance or genes, no animals that change form (metamorphosis), no hybrids. Teacher note: do not ask children to compare themselves with their parents (adoption, foster care, family separation); use plants and animals.

words: sun; moon; star; rise; set; sky; day; night
cross_subject: ela:W.1.8 (recall observations to answer a question)
notes: Use observations of the sun, moon and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted: the sun and moon seem to rise on one side of the sky, move across it and set; stars other than the sun are seen at night and not in the day. Students mark the sun's place from one window or a shadow stick at three times of day and keep a moon drawing log at home and school, extending the daily record habit of sk-weather-watch. Boundary: star patterns only as seen at night, not in the day; no Earth turning or orbit model (that is grade 5). Teacher note: never look straight at the sun; observe its position by shadows.

words: daylight; season; winter; spring; summer; fall; longer; shorter
cross_subject: math:1.MD.C.4 (organise and compare data in up to three groups)
notes: Make observations at different times of year to relate the amount of daylight to the season: is it dark or light at the same clock time (going-home time) in fall, winter and spring? The class records it on a chart and compares, finding that winter has less daylight than spring or fall. data-graph grows from the kindergarten weather chart: now a chart the class reads to compare categories. Boundary: relative amounts only, no counting hours of daylight. Needs a record kept across the year, so the unit opens in fall and closes in spring.

words: material; property; hard; soft; bendy; rough; smooth; sort
cross_subject: ela:W.2.7 (record science observations in a shared project)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation to describe and sort different materials (wood, metal, plastic, fabric, paper, rubber, glass shown not handled) by properties they can observe: colour, texture, hardness, flexibility, and whether light passes through (from s1-light-materials). Patterns: different objects can share a property; one material can be found in many objects. Students design the sorting tests (scratch, bend, press). Boundary: observable properties only, no measured mass or volume (grade 5). Teacher note: no glass or sharp metal in student hands.

words: strong; absorb; flexible; test; best; purpose; data
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (draw a bar graph of the test results)
notes: Analyse data from testing materials to decide which has the properties that best suit a purpose: which paper towel soaks up most water, which fabric is best for a raincoat, which material makes the strongest bridge deck. Students run the tests, measure in length where they measure (how far the water climbed, how far the deck bent), make a bar graph and argue for a choice. data-graph grows from s1-daylight-seasons to a bar graph students draw; structure-function grows from s1-sketch-shape: material as well as shape fits the job. Boundary: quantitative measures are length only. Teacher note: wipe up water at once.

words: piece; part; whole; take apart; build; new
cross_subject: ela:W.2.8 (recall information from experience to answer a question)
notes: Make observations to build an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces (blocks, building bricks, a set of shapes) can be taken apart and made into a new object: the same pieces, a different whole. The evidence-based account grows from s1-see-with-light. The system-model returns as parts and whole. This is the first step toward the grade 5 idea that matter is made of pieces too small to see and is not lost when things change; no particle model is introduced here.

words: heat; cool; melt; freeze; change; reverse; change back
cross_subject: ela:W.2.1 (write an opinion with reasons)
notes: Make an argument from evidence that some changes caused by heating or cooling can be reversed and some cannot: water freezes and melts back, butter or chocolate melts and hardens again; an egg once cooked, a leaf once frozen and thawed, paper once heated stay changed. The argument grows from s1-like-parents: a claim, evidence from observation and a reason. Boundary: no particle explanation (grade 5). Teacher note: all heating is done by an adult with a warm-water bath or hot plate kept out of reach, never a flame near students; check egg, dairy and other food allergies; nothing is eaten.

words: grow; sunlight; water; test; fair; change one thing; measure
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure plant height with a ruler)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation to find out whether plants need sunlight and water to grow: one set of seedlings with light and water, one in the dark, one without water, everything else kept the same. Students measure height and draw how the plants look over two to three weeks and graph the results. Tests the kindergarten claim (sk-living-needs) by experiment; that handoff skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no plant-needs expectation. Planning grows from s1-light-materials to a fair test. Boundary: one variable at a time. Teacher note: discard mouldy soil promptly; wash hands after handling soil.

words: seed; spread; pollen; pollinate; flower; depend
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure how far a model seed travels)
notes: Develop a simple model that copies what an animal does to spread seeds or carry pollen: a sock or fuzzy glove walked through a field of burr-like seeds, a pipe-cleaner "bee" that moves pollen (chalk dust or powdered drink mix) from flower to flower. The model shows a plant and an animal depending on each other (system-model). It reverses the design of s1-parts-mimic: there people copied nature; here a model copies the animal's job. Teacher note: no live bees; check pollen and dust allergies; burrs kept away from hair and eyes.

words: habitat; land; water; many kinds; diversity; survey; compare
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (picture graph of how many kinds were found in each place)
notes: Make observations of plants and animals to compare how many different kinds live in different habitats: a schoolyard survey of two spots (lawn and garden bed, or sunny and shady), then photographs and video of a pond, a forest, a desert and an ocean shore. Students count kinds, not names, and graph them. Uses the parts-and-needs reasoning of s1-parts-mimic and the system-model of sk-needs-places (that handoff skips grade 1, which has no habitat expectation). Boundary: specific plant and animal names in specific habitats are not assessed. Teacher note: outdoor survey rules (no touching unknown plants or animals, stay in sight, return anything moved); check for stinging insects and allergies.

words: land; water; hill; valley; mountain; river; lake; ocean; map
cross_subject: social-studies:ss1-landforms-waters (landforms and bodies of water named in grade 1)
notes: Develop a model (a sand-tray landscape, clay relief or picture map with a key) to show the shapes and kinds of land and bodies of water in an area: the local area first, then a contrasting one. Students find patterns (rivers run downhill to lakes or oceans). Boundary: no quantitative scaling in the model. The map key and landform words lean on social studies grade 1 and 2 map work; science adds the model as a thing to reason with. No in-band assumes: kindergarten and grade 1 science have no landform expectation.

words: ocean; river; lake; pond; ice; glacier; solid; liquid
cross_subject: ela:W.2.8 (gather information from provided sources to answer a question)
notes: Obtain information from texts, maps and video to find where water is found on Earth (oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, ice and snow) and that it can be solid or liquid. Connects to the solid and liquid water of s2-heat-cool-change. The obtaining-information practice grows from s1-parent-offspring: now students record facts from two sources on one chart. Boundary: no water cycle (grade 5 and middle school) and no amounts.

words: quick; slow; earthquake; volcano; erosion; landslide; change; time
cross_subject: ela:RI.2.3 (describe how events in a text connect)
notes: Use information from several sources (photographs, video, simple texts) to give evidence that some Earth events happen quickly (a volcano erupting, an earthquake, a landslide, a flood) and others slowly (a canyon carved by a river, a rock worn smooth). Introduces stability-change (a model name added by this band for the stability and change crosscutting concept, which no shared name covers): the land looks the same day to day but changes, fast or slow. Builds on sk-forecast-severe (severe weather as an event people prepare for; skips grade 1, which has no Earth-events expectation) and on the reading of sources in s1-parent-offspring. Boundary: no measured time scales. Teacher note: disaster images can upset children who have lived through one; choose images without injured people and stress helpers and safety.

words: erosion; wind; water; wall; windbreak; roots; protect
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure how much sand washed away in centimetres)
notes: Compare several solutions designed to slow or stop wind or water from changing the shape of the land: in a tray of sand and soil, walls, rock barriers, grass mats and stick windbreaks are tested against poured water or a fan, and the class measures how far the land wore back. Uses stability-change from s2-fast-slow-events and the design-cycle from s1-signal-device; the comparison of two tested designs is the work of s2-compare-designs. Teacher note: fans run only on low with fingers clear; water spills are wiped at once to stop slips; wash hands after soil.

words: compare; better; worse; strength; weakness; test; data
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (bar graph to compare two designs)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-3, done in full here: analyse data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem and say what each does well and poorly. Practised through s2-erosion-solutions (two barrier designs) and s2-best-material (two materials). Grows from kindergarten, where students only judged whether one design worked (sk-ramp-design), and grade 1, where they sketched and explained one design (s1-sketch-shape). The full K-2 design-cycle is now: define the problem, sketch, build, test, compare. Grades 3 to 5 add criteria, constraints and fair tests of many solutions.
